nameStory: The genus name Titanoeca comes from Greek mythology, referencing the powerful Titans who were said to be giants of incredible strength. This name hints at these spiders' robust build and their reputation as skilled hunters rather than delicate web-spinners.
description: The American Rock Weaver is a small, sturdy spider that belongs to a specialized family of hunters. These compact spiders have a somewhat flattened appearance and typically measure around 3-6mm in body length. Unlike many spiders that rely heavily on webs to catch prey, rock weavers are active hunters that build simple retreat webs under rocks and bark rather than elaborate snares.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and somewhat flattened spider with a sturdy build, feeling solid rather than delicate when observed closely

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates simple, sheet-like retreat webs under rocks or bark rather than elaborate catching webs

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider with body length typically 3-6mm, about the size of a pencil eraser

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active hunter that moves with quick, darting motions rather than waiting passively in a web

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight eyes arranged in two rows, with the front eyes appearing slightly larger and more prominent

habitat: American Rock Weavers prefer rocky areas, stone walls, and wooded environments where they can find crevices and gaps to hide in during the day. Look for them under loose bark, between rocks, or in stone foundations of old buildings. They seem to favor areas with some moisture but good drainage, often in mixed hardwood forests throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots to hunt and mate. Look for their small retreat webs appearing under rocks and bark.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily spotted hunting at night. Egg sacs may be found in their silk-lined retreats during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue hunting into early fall, with spiderlings dispersing from egg sacs. Activity begins to slow as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults and juveniles overwinter in protected crevices, remaining largely inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being called 'Rock Weavers,' these spiders are actually more like tiny lions than traditional web-spinners – they use their silk mainly to line cozy dens rather than trap prey, preferring to hunt by stalking and pouncing on their victims in true predator style.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small ground spiders or sac spiders, but rock weavers have a distinctly more robust, flattened appearance and their retreat webs are typically found in rockier locations rather than in vegetation or corners of buildings.
contextualKnowledge: The Titanoecidae family is relatively small and specialized, with rock weavers representing an interesting evolutionary strategy between web-building and hunting spiders – they're essentially homebodies who venture out to hunt rather than waiting for dinner to come to them.
compareHints: As the only known Titanoeca species documented in New England, comparisons must be made to other small hunting spiders in the region. Rock weavers can be distinguished from ground spiders by their more flattened profile and preference for rocky retreats, and from sac spiders by their less elongated body shape and different web structure.
